Short version: (1) You almost certainly still have to answer the lawsuit — a limitations defense is NOT automatic; if you don't raise it in a written answer, you can lose by default even on a stale debt. (2) Your written answer was due Tuesday, September 15, 2026, so you are about two days late as of today (9/17/2026) — file an answer TODAY, because in Texas justice court a late answer filed before the judge signs a default judgment normally stops the default. (3) Whether the debt is actually too old is a close call that turns on one fact I don't have (see below), but you appear to have a genuinely strong limitations argument, especially because of the long delay in serving you.

DEADLINE MATH (Tex. R. Civ. P. 502.5(a)): an answer is due 'on or before the end of the 14th day after the date the defendant was served.' You were served Tuesday, September 1, 2026. September 1 + 14 days = Tuesday, September 15, 2026. That day is not a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, so no extension applies. Today is September 17, 2026 — 2 days past due. Under Rule 503.1 the plaintiff can ask for a default judgment once the answer date passes, but the court generally cannot grant a default if an answer is on file when the judgment is signed. So: file a short written answer with the Harris County justice court clerk immediately (in person or by the court's e-filing/email), keep a stamped copy, and mail/serve a copy on the plaintiff's lawyer. Your answer can be a general denial, but you should expressly plead the affirmative defenses of (a) the four-year statute of limitations and (b) lack of due diligence in service (Tex. R. Civ. P. 94; Tex. R. Civ. P. 502.5). If a default judgment has already been signed, you have 14 days from the date it was signed to file a motion for new trial (Rule 505.3) and 21 days from signing to appeal for a new trial de novo in county court (Rule 506.1) — check the docket today.

LIMITATIONS MATH (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §§ 16.004(a)(3), 16.051 — 4 years; Tex. Fin. Code § 392.307, which bars a debt buyer from suing after the limitations period and provides that a later payment does not revive an expired period):
- Last payment March 2021 + 4 years = March 2025
- First missed payment April 2021 + 4 years = April 2025
- Charge-off / demand for the full balance November 2021 + 4 years = November 2025
- Petition file-stamped July 14, 2025

So: if the clock started with your April 2021 default (or the March 2021 last payment), it ran out around March–April 2025 and the July 14, 2025 filing was already too late. If the clock instead started when the issuer charged off the account and accelerated the whole balance in November 2021, the July 14, 2025 filing was inside the four years. Which accrual date controls depends on the terms of the cardholder agreement (i.e., whether the full balance became due automatically on default or only upon the issuer's acceleration/demand), and on any governing-law clause in that agreement. That is the fact I am missing, so I am not going to tell you the debt is or is not time-barred.

IMPORTANT SECOND POINT IN YOUR FAVOR: in Texas, merely filing the petition stops the clock only if the plaintiff then uses reasonable diligence in serving you; if not, the suit is treated as 'brought' on the date of service (Proulx v. Wells, 235 S.W.3d 213 (Tex. 2007); Gant v. DeLeon, 786 S.W.2d 259 (Tex. 1990)). Here the petition was filed July 14, 2025 and you were served September 1, 2026 — about 13.5 months (414 days) later. If the court finds no diligent effort to serve you, the effective suit date is September 1, 2026, which is past four years from every possible accrual date (including November 2021 + 4 = November 2025). Whether the plaintiff's explanation for the delay amounts to due diligence is a discretionary, fact-bound ruling by the judge, so I can't predict it — but it is worth raising.

What to do now, in order: (1) file the written answer today pleading limitations and lack of diligent service; (2) request a copy of the cardholder agreement and the plaintiff's chain-of-title/account documents (in justice court you generally need the judge's permission for formal discovery, Rule 500.9); (3) get a licensed Texas consumer-defense attorney or a local legal-aid office (e.g., Lone Star Legal Aid in Houston) to evaluate the accrual date, the governing-law clause, and whether the debt buyer's collection suit on a possibly time-barred debt also gives you claims under Tex. Fin. Code § 392.307 and the federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. §§ 1692e, 1692f) — the FDCPA has a 1-year suit deadline from the violation, which for the filing/service would run from July 14, 2025 / September 1, 2026, so don't sit on that either.
answer.missing_fact: The cardholder agreement's default/acceleration (and governing-law) terms — i.e., whether the entire balance became due on your April 2021 default (clock expires ~April 2025, so the July 14, 2025 filing was late) or only upon the issuer's November 2021 charge-off/acceleration demand (clock ran to ~November 2025, so the filing was timely).

answer.answer:
Short answer: your deadline depends on a date you don't have yet — the date the process server MAILED a copy of the summons and complaint to your apartment. Under California law, leaving the papers with your adult son is only half of "substituted service." Code of Civil Procedure § 415.20(b) requires the server to (1) leave the papers with a competent household member 18 or older at your dwelling AND (2) thereafter mail a copy by first-class mail to you at the address where the papers were left. Service is then deemed complete on the 10th day after that mailing. Your response (answer, demurrer, motion to strike, etc.) is due 30 days after service is complete (CCP § 412.20(a)(3)).

The math, using the earliest possible mailing date (the same day, Thursday Aug 20, 2026):
• Mailing date: Aug 20, 2026
• + 10 days = Aug 30, 2026 → service deemed complete
• + 30 days = Sept 29, 2026 (Aug 30 + 1 day = Aug 31; 29 more days = Sept 29, a Tuesday, not a holiday, so no extension under CCP §§ 12, 12a)
So the EARLIEST your answer could be due is Tuesday, September 29, 2026. That date has not passed — today is Sept 17, 2026, which is 12 days before it.

If the mailing happened later, the deadline moves later. General formula: mailing date + 10 days = service complete; + 30 days = response due; if that last day falls on a weekend or court holiday, it rolls to the next court day (CCP §§ 12, 12a). Examples: mailed Aug 24 → complete Sept 3 → due Oct 3, which is a Saturday, so Monday Oct 5, 2026. Mailed Aug 27 → complete Sept 6 → due Oct 6, 2026.

If no copy was ever mailed, substituted service was never completed and no response clock has started — but do NOT rely on that assumption. The collector's proof of service will almost certainly recite a mailing date, and the court will treat that date as valid unless you move to quash service (CCP § 418.10, which must be filed on or before the date your response is due). Meanwhile you could be defaulted (CCP § 585).

What to do now, this week:
1. Check your mail/anything your son set aside for an envelope from the process server or law firm.
2. Look up the case on the superior court's online case index or call the clerk and ask for the register of actions / the filed proof of service (Judicial Council form POS-010). It states the exact mailing date. That single date fixes your deadline.
3. Until you confirm it, calendar Tuesday, September 29, 2026 as your working deadline — that is the earliest it can be, so filing by then is safe under every scenario.
4. If you need more time, you can ask the plaintiff's attorney in writing for a stipulated extension (common, often 15–30 days) and get it confirmed in writing and filed, or file your answer early. There is no automatic extension.

Filing a general denial (form PLD-050 for limited civil cases under § 431.30(d)) plus any affirmative defenses (e.g., statute of limitations — 4 years for written contract under CCP § 337, or the account-stated/open-book rules) preserves your rights; a fee waiver (form FW-001) is available if you can't afford the filing fee. Nothing here says your deadline has passed or that you lack defenses — you appear to still be within the response window.

Short version: the safest course is to get your written dispute postmarked no later than Thursday, October 8, 2026, and ideally in the next few days. Here is why, and why I can't pin the exact last day without one fact from you.

1) The rule. Under the FDCPA, 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b), if you notify the collector IN WRITING within 30 days AFTER YOU RECEIVED the validation notice that you dispute the debt (or any part of it), the collector must cease collection of the debt until it mails you verification. The 30 days runs from your receipt of the letter, not from the date it was mailed — so the exact deadline depends on the day the envelope actually arrived, which is the one fact I don't have.

2) Earliest possible deadline (assume fastest delivery). The letter was mailed Friday, September 4, 2026. Saturday Sept 5 and Sunday Sept 6 are a weekend and Monday Sept 7 was Labor Day (a federal holiday with no regular mail delivery), so the earliest realistic delivery day was Tuesday, September 8, 2026. Counting 30 days from Sept 8: Sept 8 + 22 days = Sept 30; 30 − 22 = 8 more days = October 8, 2026 (a Thursday). So if you received it on Sept 8, your last day is Thursday, October 8, 2026.

3) Latest deadline under the CFPB's 'assumed receipt' rule. Regulation F, 12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(b)(5), lets a collector assume you received the validation information on a date at least five days after it provided the notice, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal public holidays. Counting forward from Friday Sept 4: skip Sat 9/5, Sun 9/6, and Labor Day Mon 9/7; day 1 = Tue 9/8, day 2 = Wed 9/9, day 3 = Thu 9/10, day 4 = Fri 9/11, skip 9/12–9/13, day 5 = Monday, September 14, 2026. Thirty days after Sept 14: Sept 14 + 16 days = Sept 30; 30 − 16 = 14 more days = Wednesday, October 14, 2026. That is the end of the 'validation period' if the collector uses the regulatory assumption, and during that period Reg F also limits what the collector can do (e.g., 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)(i), § 1006.38).

4) Practical bottom line. Because a collector could argue the 30 days ran from your actual (earlier) receipt date, do not rely on October 14. Mail your written dispute so it is postmarked on or before Thursday, October 8, 2026 — sooner is better. Send it by certified mail, return receipt requested (or use the collector's designated email/portal if it offered one), keep a copy and the tracking proof, and state plainly: 'I dispute this debt and request verification of the debt and the name and address of the original creditor.' The dispute must be in writing to trigger the stop-collection-until-verification duty; an oral dispute does not trigger it under § 1692g(b).

5) If you miss the 30 days. You are not out of options: you can still dispute the debt, the collector still may not make false statements about it (15 U.S.C. § 1692e), you can tell it in writing to stop contacting you (15 U.S.C. § 1692c(c)), and you can dispute the tradeline with the credit bureaus under 15 U.S.C. § 1681i. Also, a written dispute means the collector must report the debt as disputed if it furnishes it to the bureaus (15 U.S.C. § 1692e(8)).

You can also simply call or email the agency and ask it to re-send the notice page stating the 'dispute by' date — Reg F requires that date to be on the notice, and the agency's own stated date is strong evidence in your favor if there is ever a dispute about timeliness.

Short answer: No. In Texas, your ordinary W-2 wages cannot be garnished to collect a private judgment on a credit-card debt, and the lawyer's '25% like the federal rules allow' statement misstates the law.

Why:

1. Texas is one of a handful of states that flatly prohibits wage garnishment for ordinary consumer debts. The Texas Constitution, art. XVI, § 28, provides that 'no current wages for personal service shall ever be subject to garnishment, except for the enforcement of court-ordered child support payments or spousal maintenance.' Tex. Prop. Code § 42.001(b)(1) likewise makes current wages for personal services exempt from seizure, with no cap or percentage. A judgment creditor cannot serve your Dallas employer with a writ ordering it to withhold any part of your paycheck for this judgment.

2. The only exceptions are the ones your facts rule out: court-ordered child support, spousal maintenance, certain federal obligations (federal student loans, federal taxes, other federal debts), and court-ordered restitution. A debt buyer's credit-card judgment is none of these.

3. Short answer: nobody can promise you the judge will set the judgment aside — that is a discretionary ruling by the trial judge, and only a licensed Texas attorney who reads your file can assess your merits. But the hard deadline is very real and very close: your motion for new trial is due Thursday, September 24, 2026, which is 7 days from today. Do not let that date pass.

DATE MATH
- Judgment signed: Tuesday, August 25, 2026.
- Motion for new trial / motion to set aside default: due within 30 days after the judgment is signed (Tex. R. Civ. P. 329b(a), 320). Aug 25 + 6 days = Aug 31; + 24 days = Sept 24. So the deadline is Thursday, September 24, 2026. That is a regular business day, so there is no weekend/holiday rollover.
- TRCP 306a(4) sometimes restarts that 30 days for people who never got notice of the judgment, but that does not help you: you learned of it two days after signing (Aug 27), well within the 20-day window, so your clock runs from Aug 25.
- Court's plenary power: if you file a timely motion for new trial, the judge can act until 75 days after signing (Nov 8, 2026, when it would be overruled by operation of law if not ruled on) and retains plenary power for 30 days after that (to about Dec 8, 2026) (TRCP 329b(c), (e)).
- Notice of appeal: 30 days after judgment (Sept 24, 2026) if you file nothing, extended to 90 days (Monday, November 23, 2026) if you timely file a motion for new trial (Tex. R. App. P. 26.1(a)).
- Backstops if you miss Sept 24: a restricted appeal within 6 months of the judgment, i.e., by about February 25, 2027 — but ONLY if you did not participate in the hearing and did NOT file a timely post-judgment motion (Tex. R. App. P. 30); and an equitable bill of review, generally within 4 years (TRCP 329b(f); Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 16.051). Both are harder and slower than a motion for new trial, so use the motion for new trial.

THE LEGAL STANDARD THE JUDGE WILL APPLY
Because this is a county court at law, the regular Rules of Civil Procedure apply, and a no-answer default is set aside under the three-part Craddock test (Craddock v. Sunshine Bus Lines, 134 S.W.2d 388 (Tex. 1939)):
1) Your failure to answer was not intentional or the result of conscious indifference, but due to accident or mistake — a three-week hospitalization is exactly the kind of excuse courts accept, if you prove it;
2) Your motion sets up a meritorious defense — payment in full is a recognized affirmative defense, and you only have to allege facts that would constitute a defense and support them with prima facie proof (your 2023 bank records); you do not have to prove you win; and
3) Granting a new trial will cause no delay or injury to the plaintiff — you show this by stating you are ready for immediate trial and offering to reimburse the plaintiff's costs in obtaining the default.
When all three are met, Texas appellate courts have held a trial court abuses its discretion by refusing a new trial (Dolgencorp of Tex. v. Lerma, 288 S.W.3d 922 (Tex. 2009)). So your facts line up well — but whether the judge credits your proof is still the judge's call, and I will not predict it.

WHAT TO DO IN THE NEXT 7 DAYS
1) File, before Sept 24, a "Motion for New Trial and Motion to Set Aside Default Judgment," verified or supported by your sworn affidavit. Attach: hospital/admission-discharge records covering the answer deadline, and your 2023 bank/payment records showing the debt was paid. Expressly plead all three Craddock elements, state you are ready for trial now, and offer to pay the plaintiff's costs of obtaining the default.
2) File your Answer at the same time (general denial plus the affirmative defense of payment; also consider statute of limitations and lack of standing/ownership of the account).
3) Request an oral hearing and get it set inside the court's plenary window.
4) Ask for a stay of execution. Filing a motion for new trial does NOT automatically stop collection — the judgment creditor can abstract the judgment and try to freeze bank accounts. In Texas, current wages are exempt from garnishment for ordinary consumer debt (Tex. Const. art. XVI § 28), but bank accounts are not automatically protected.
5) In parallel, send your proof of payment to the debt buyer's lawyer and ask them to agree to set the judgment aside. An agreed motion is the fastest, cheapest route, and collectors often agree when the debt was in fact paid.
6) Do not file a restricted appeal instead — filing a timely motion for new trial forfeits that option, and the motion for new trial is the better tool now.
7) Separate issue worth asking a consumer lawyer about: suing to collect a debt that was already paid can violate the federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. § 1692e(2), (10)) and the Texas Debt Collection Act (Tex. Fin. Code ch. 392). FDCPA claims have a 1-year deadline from the violation (15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d)) — if the suit was filed within the last year, that clock is running too.

Get a Texas consumer-defense attorney on this today; many handle default set-asides on a flat fee, and legal aid in Dallas County may help. The one thing you cannot do is wait past September 24, 2026.

Dolgencorp of Texas, Inc. v. Lerma, 288 S.W.3d 922 (Tex. 2009)

Short answer: probably not under the federal FDCPA/Regulation F on these facts — but you may well have a claim under California's Rosenthal Act, which does reach original creditors.

1) Why the FDCPA/Reg F likely does not apply here. The FDCPA regulates "debt collectors," which the statute defines as people who collect debts owed to *another*. A creditor collecting its own debt, in its own name, with its own employees, is expressly outside that definition (15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6)(A) and (F)(ii)). Two exceptions that sometimes bring a creditor in do not appear to fit your facts: (a) the creditor uses a name other than its own that suggests a third party is calling — you say they call under the bank's own name; and (b) the entity acquired the debt after it was already in default — you say the bank issued the card and has not sold it. Regulation F, including the 7-calls-in-7-days rule you are referring to (12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)(i)), applies only to "debt collectors" as defined in 12 C.F.R. § 1006.2(i), which tracks the FDCPA. So the federal 7-in-7 presumption does not, by its own force, bind a first-party bank collections department.

2) Why you may still have a California claim. California's Rosenthal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act defines "debt collector" much more broadly — a person who, in the ordinary course of business, regularly, *on behalf of himself or herself* or others, engages in debt collection (Cal. Civ. Code § 1788.2(c)). A national bank's in-house collections unit collecting its own consumer credit card debt generally falls within that definition. Two routes:
   • Rosenthal's own harassment provisions: Civ. Code § 1788.11(d) (causing a telephone to ring repeatedly or continuously to annoy the person called) and § 1788.11(e) (communicating by telephone with such frequency as is unreasonable and constitutes harassment under the circumstances). Ten calls in seven days about one account is the kind of pattern that supports such a claim, though it is fact-dependent.
   • Civ. Code § 1788.17, which makes Rosenthal-covered collectors comply with 15 U.S.C. §§ 1692b–1692j, including § 1692d(5) (repeated calls intended to annoy, abuse, or harass). Whether § 1788.17 also imports Regulation F's 7-in-7 *presumption* (as opposed to the statutory text) is an unsettled question that California and federal courts have not uniformly resolved; do not assume the presumption automatically applies to you.

3) This is a discretionary, fact-intensive merits call. Whether a given call volume is "unreasonable" harassment, and whether Reg F's presumption travels into Rosenthal, are judgment calls for a court/jury and for a licensed California consumer attorney — I can't predict the outcome. What helps: call logs, times of day, whether they called after you answered and told them to stop or to call at different times, whether they called your workplace or third parties, and what was said.

4) Hard deadlines (date math). Your calls occurred in the seven days ending today: roughly 2026-09-10 through 2026-09-17. Both the FDCPA and the Rosenthal Act carry a one-year limitations period (15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d); Cal. Civ. Code § 1788.30(f), which runs one year from the date of the violation). So the earliest of these calls would need suit filed by about 2026-09-10 + 1 year = 2027-09-10, and the most recent by about 2027-09-17. Nothing here is time-barred — you have roughly a year, but each call has its own clock, so do not wait.

5) Two other angles worth raising with counsel: (a) the TCPA, if the calls are to your cell phone using a prerecorded/artificial voice or an autodialer and you have revoked consent in writing or orally — statutory damages of $500–$1,500 per call; and (b) Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200, using the Rosenthal violation as a predicate. Also, a written request that they stop calling (keep a copy, send it in a trackable way) both protects you going forward and strengthens the record.

6) Practical note: Rosenthal statutory damages are $100–$1,000 plus actual damages and attorney's fees for a willful and knowing violation (Civ. Code § 1788.30(a)–(c)). National-bank preemption arguments are sometimes raised against state debt-collection claims, but courts have generally allowed Rosenthal claims against national banks' collection conduct.

Short answer: No. Under the FDCPA you did NOT have to use the word "dispute." A written request for the name and address of the original creditor, made within the 30-day validation window, independently triggers the collector's duty to stop collecting.

The statute, 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b), says that if within the 30-day period in § 1692g(a) the consumer notifies the collector in writing that the debt is disputed **or requests the name and address of the original creditor**, the debt collector "shall cease collection of the debt, or any disputed portion thereof, until the debt collector obtains verification of the debt or a copy of a judgment, or the name and address of the original creditor, and a copy of such verification or judgment, or name and address of the original creditor, is mailed to the consumer." The CFPB's Regulation F says the same thing at 12 C.F.R. § 1006.38(d)(1)–(2): for an original-creditor request, the collector must cease collection until it mails the original creditor's name and address to you.

Date arithmetic (using the day you received the validation notice as Day 0):
- Day 0 = date you received the validation notice.
- Your 30-day validation period ran Day 1 through Day 30.
- You mailed the request on Day 12. 12 < 30, so the request was made inside the window (and the facts say the agency received it, which on ordinary mail timing would be roughly Day 14–17, also inside the window).

Consequences:
1. From the moment they received your letter, the agency was required to stop collection activity on that debt until it mails you the original creditor's name and address. Four collection calls plus a second letter demanding payment, with no original-creditor information provided, are collection activity and on these facts appear to violate § 1692g(b) and 12 C.F.R. § 1006.38(d)(2). Repeated calls in that posture can also support claims under § 1692d (harassment/abuse) or § 1692f (unfair practices) depending on their number, timing and content.
2. Your failure to say the word "dispute" costs you nothing here. Separately, § 1692g(c) provides that a consumer's failure to dispute a debt may not be construed by any court as an admission of liability.
3. Practical step: keep the postmark/mailing proof, any certified-mail receipt, your phone log with dates and times of the four calls, and both letters. You may also send a short written follow-up that (a) states the debt is disputed and (b) repeats the request for the original creditor's name and address, and you can send a written request under § 1692c(c) that they cease communicating with you altogether.

Deadline you must watch: an FDCPA lawsuit must be brought "within one year from the date on which the violation occurs" — 15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d). Each offending call and letter is generally its own violation with its own one-year clock. Today is 2026-09-17, so any violation that occurred on or after 2025-09-17 is within one year as of today; violations older than that may be outside the private-action limitations period (the Supreme Court held in Rotkiske v. Klemm, 589 U.S. 8 (2019), that the clock runs from the violation, not from discovery, though it left open a possible fraud-based equitable tolling argument). Because I don't have the actual calendar dates of the validation notice, your letter, the four calls, or the second letter, I can't tell you the exact filing deadline — write those dates down and give them to a lawyer promptly.

Remedies if a violation is proven: actual damages, additional statutory damages up to $1,000 per action, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees (§ 1692k(a)). You can also complain to the CFPB and your state attorney general. Whether a court finds these particular calls violated the Act, and how much it awards, is a discretionary judicial determination — I can't predict it, and the merits should be reviewed by a licensed consumer-protection attorney (many take FDCPA cases on a fee-shifting basis at no upfront cost).

Short answer: the 7-in-7 rule is not a 'per phone number' rule. It counts every call the collector places to *you* about that one debt, no matter which of your numbers it dials. Nine calls in seven days about a single credit-card debt therefore puts the collector over the limit and creates a presumption that it violated the law.

How the rule works (Regulation F, 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)(i)): a debt collector is presumed to violate the FDCPA's prohibition on harassing/abusive repeated calls (15 U.S.C. § 1692d(5)) if it places telephone calls to *a person* more than seven times within any seven-consecutive-day period in connection with the collection of a particular debt. The trigger is calls 'to a person,' not calls to a particular device or line. Nothing in the rule distinguishes cell phones from landlines, work lines, or home lines; the CFPB deliberately wrote it around the person and the particular debt. (Consent is also irrelevant to this count — the 7-in-7 cap applies whether or not you ever consented to calls; consent matters to the TCPA, a different statute.)

The date math: Monday, September 7, 2026 through Sunday, September 13, 2026 is exactly seven consecutive days (Sept 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 = 7 days). Calls placed in that window: 7 (cell) + 2 (work direct line) = 9. 9 − 7 = 2 calls over the cap. Because the window is a rolling one, any seven-consecutive-day slice containing eight or more calls also triggers the presumption.

Two technical points that could affect the count:
• Excluded calls, § 1006.14(b)(3). Certain calls don't count: calls placed to your attorney, a consumer reporting agency, the creditor or the creditor's/collector's attorney; calls placed with your prior consent given directly to the collector during a phone conversation (you had none); and — the one to watch — 'telephone calls placed to a person that are not connected to the dialed number.' Under the Official Interpretations, that exclusion covers calls that never go through (e.g., a technical/network failure), *not* calls that ring through and simply go unanswered. Your facts say the calls were unanswered, not that they failed to connect, so on these facts all nine count. If the collector's dialer logs show some calls never connected at all, subtract those; you are over the cap as long as at least eight connected.
• The presumption is rebuttable. Exceeding seven calls creates a presumption of violation, not an automatic judgment; the collector can try to show in court that its conduct was not harassment, oppression, or abuse under § 1692d(5) (just as staying under seven gives it a presumption of compliance, § 1006.14(b)(2)(ii)). Whether a court accepts a rebuttal is a discretionary merits call — that should be evaluated by a licensed FDCPA attorney, not predicted here.

A separate possible claim on the two work calls: § 1692c(a)(3) bars a collector from calling you at your place of employment if it knows or has reason to know your employer prohibits such calls. I can't tell from your facts whether your employer prohibits personal/collection calls or whether the collector knew that, so I'm not opining on that claim — but if your employer does prohibit it and you or someone told the collector (or it otherwise had reason to know), each work call is independently actionable. Also, § 1692c(a)(1) bars calls at unusual/inconvenient times (presumed before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. your local time), so note the time of each call.

Deadline to act: FDCPA suits must be brought within one year of the violation, 15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d). Counting from the individual calls, the earliest of your nine calls (Sept 7, 2026) runs to on or about September 7, 2027, and the last (Sept 13, 2026) to on or about September 13, 2027. Today is September 17, 2026, so you are well inside that period — but don't let it slip. Remedies under § 1692k(a) can include actual damages, statutory damages up to $1,000 per action, and costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

Practical steps: save your phone logs and any screenshots/voicemails showing date, time, number called and number calling; send a written request that they stop calling (a § 1692c(c) cease-communication notice) and, if applicable, tell them in writing your employer prohibits calls at work; and consider a written dispute within 30 days of their validation notice to trigger § 1692g verification duties.

No — that's only half the rule, and on these facts the calls look presumptively unlawful.

Regulation F (12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)), which implements FDCPA § 806(5) (15 U.S.C. § 1692d(5)), has TWO call-frequency triggers for a particular debt, not one:

1. The 7-in-7 trigger: more than 7 calls in 7 consecutive days. You're right that 5 calls does not exceed 7, so this prong was not crossed.

2. The 7-days-after-a-conversation trigger: § 1006.14(b)(2)(i)(B) / (b)(2)(ii)(B) — a collector is presumed to violate the law if it places a call about that debt within 7 consecutive days AFTER having had a telephone conversation with the person about that debt. There is no exception for a conversation the consumer started; what matters is that a telephone conversation about the debt occurred.

Date math:
- Telephone conversation: Tuesday, September 8, 2026.
- The 7 consecutive days after that conversation: Sept 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 2026. The window closes at the end of Tuesday, September 15, 2026; the first call that would fall outside it is Wednesday, September 16, 2026.
- Calls placed: Sept 9 (day 1), Sept 10 (day 2), Sept 11 (day 3), Sept 12 (day 4), Sept 14 (day 6). All five fall inside the post-conversation window.

So the very first call on September 9 already triggered the presumption, and each of the other four did too. Because there is only one debt here (one medical account), all five calls count against the same limit — the per-debt counting rule doesn't help the agency.

Two important qualifications:
- The presumption is rebuttable. Under § 1006.14(b)(2)(ii) a court presumes the collector violated the law, but the collector can try to rebut it with evidence. Whether a particular court finds it rebutted is a discretionary merits call — that's for a licensed attorney to evaluate, not something I can predict.
- Certain calls don't count as 'calls placed' under § 1006.14(b)(3): calls made with your prior consent given directly to the collector during the 7-day window (you say you never asked them to call back, so this doesn't apply), calls made in response to your request for information, calls that never connect to the dialed number (e.g., dropped before ringing), and calls to your attorney, a credit bureau, the creditor, or lawyers for either. If some of those five 'calls' never actually connected, those particular ones would drop out of the count — but the post-conversation rule would still be triggered by any one that did connect.

Deadline you should know: a private FDCPA suit must be filed within one year of the violation, 15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d). Counting from the earliest call (Sept 9, 2026), that is September 9, 2027; from the last call (Sept 14, 2026), September 14, 2027. Today is September 17, 2026, so you have roughly a year — nothing has expired. Statutory damages up to $1,000 per action plus actual damages, costs and attorney's fees may be available (§ 1692k(a)).

One more practical point for you: you can stop the calls now by sending a written notice under 15 U.S.C. § 1692c(c) telling them to cease communication, or by telling them a particular time/place is inconvenient under § 1692c(a)(1). Keep your phone records — they are the proof of the five calls and the Sept 8 conversation.

Short answer: I can't tell you yet, because the one fact that decides it — the date the letter was sent or received — is missing. But do NOT assume you're out of time, and do not assume disputing is pointless even if the 30 days ran.

How the 30 days is actually measured
• Under the FDCPA, the 30-day dispute window runs from the date you RECEIVED the validation notice, not from today and not from when your mother handed it to you. 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(a)–(b).
• Under the CFPB's Regulation F, the 'validation period' starts when the collector provides the notice and ends 30 days after you receive it, and you are ASSUMED to have received it on the fifth day (excluding Sundays and legal public holidays) after the collector sent it. 12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(b)(5).

Worked examples using today's date (September 17, 2026):
• If the collector mailed it August 1, 2026: count 5 days excluding Sundays/holidays — Aug 3 (1), Aug 4 (2), Aug 5 (3), Aug 6 (4), Aug 7 (5). Assumed receipt = Aug 7, 2026. Aug 7 + 30 days = September 6, 2026. That window would have closed before today.
• If the collector mailed it September 1, 2026: Sept 2 (1), Sept 3 (2), Sept 4 (3), Sept 5 (4) — Sept 6 is a Sunday and Sept 7, 2026 is Labor Day, both excluded — Sept 8 (5). Assumed receipt = Sept 8, 2026. Sept 8 + 30 days = October 8, 2026. That window would still be OPEN today, with three weeks left.
Same letter, different mailing date, opposite answer. So find the date first.

How to find the date
1. Most Reg F-compliant validation notices state a specific calendar date for the end of the validation period (the model notice says something like 'write to us by [date]') — re-read the letter for any date, including an 'itemization date' or a reference/account date. 12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(c)(3), (c)(4).
2. Call or write the collector and ask for the date the notice was mailed and a re-send of the letter. If the notice truly contained no date at all, that may itself be a Regulation F compliance problem worth having a lawyer look at.
3. Check your credit reports — a collection tradeline often shows the date the account was placed/reported.

What happens under each alternative
• If you are still inside the window: send a WRITTEN dispute (and a written request for the name/address of the original creditor) before the deadline, by a method you can prove — certified mail, return receipt, or the collector's e-mail/portal with a saved confirmation. The collector must then cease collection until it mails you verification. 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b); 12 C.F.R. § 1006.38(b)–(d).
• If the window has closed: you are NOT stuck with the debt and you have not admitted anything. Missing the 30 days only costs you the automatic 'stop collection until verified' protection. You may still (a) dispute in writing at any time — many collectors will still verify, (b) tell them in writing to stop contacting you entirely (15 U.S.C. § 1692c(c)), (c) dispute the tradeline with each credit bureau, which triggers a mandatory investigation by the furnisher (15 U.S.C. § 1681i, § 1681s-2(b)), and (d) defend fully on the merits if you are ever sued — 'this is not my debt' is a complete defense regardless of the 30 days. It is also still illegal for the collector to misrepresent the debt or to collect an amount not owed. 15 U.S.C. §§ 1692e, 1692f.

Because you say the debt is not yours, dispute in writing now either way, and say expressly that you do not owe it and that you are disputing it (state that you are disputing within the validation period if the date turns out to support that). Keep proof of the date you send it.

One other clock to keep in mind: if the collector did something unlawful, an FDCPA damages claim must be filed within one year of the violation. 15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d). So pinning down the letter's date matters for that too. Nothing here tells me any deadline has actually passed.

Short answer: No — please do not ignore this lawsuit. Your two-year theory is very likely wrong, and if you do nothing you will almost certainly have a default judgment entered against you, with wage garnishment and bank levies to follow.

1) Why the 2-year 'oral contract' rule does not fit your facts. California has a 2-year limit for oral contracts (Code Civ. Proc. § 339(1)) and a 4-year limit for contracts 'founded upon an instrument in writing' (§ 337(a)). A credit card agreement you accepted online is treated as a WRITTEN contract, not an oral one. Two reasons: (a) California law does not require a handwritten signature for a contract to count as 'written' — what matters is that the terms are set out in writing and that you manifested assent (here, by clicking through the terms and then using the card for two years); and (b) under California's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, an electronic record satisfies any rule of law requiring a writing, and an electronic signature satisfies any signature requirement (Civ. Code §§ 1633.7(a)–(d), 1633.9). The fact that you no longer have the documents does not convert the agreement into an oral one — it just means the plaintiff has to prove the terms. Separately, credit card suits are commonly pleaded as an 'open book account,' which also carries a 4-year limit running from the last item in the account (Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a)(2)). Either way, the number is 4 years, not 2.

2) The date math. Your first missed payment (the breach that starts the clock) was in May 2023. May 2023 + 4 years = May 2027. The debt buyer filed in August 2026, which is roughly 9 months BEFORE the limitations period would expire. Even measured from the later charge-off in 2023, the suit is early, not late. So a statute-of-limitations defense on these facts is not a winner, and 'ignoring it' is the worst option.

3) Your real deadline — this is the urgent part. You were personally served on September 10, 2026. Under Code Civ. Proc. § 412.20(a)(3), you have 30 days after personal service to file a written response (an Answer or a demurrer/motion). Counting: September 10 is day 0; the remaining days in September (11–30) are 20 days; you need 10 more, which lands on October 10, 2026. October 10, 2026 falls on a Saturday, so under Code Civ. Proc. § 12a and § 135 the deadline rolls to the next court day — nominally Monday, October 12, 2026. Because there is some variation in whether courts are closed on the second Monday in October, do not rely on that one-day rollover: treat Friday, October 9, 2026 as your practical deadline and file by then. Note that the 30 days is NOT extended by mail-service rules (Code Civ. Proc. § 1013 does not apply to personal service). If you miss it, the plaintiff can request a default and then a default judgment (Code Civ. Proc. §§ 585, 586).

4) What to do instead of ignoring it. File an Answer (Judicial Council form PLD-C-010 for a contract case, or a general denial on form PLD-050 if the complaint is unverified and the demand is under $1,000 — otherwise use the Answer form and deny the allegations, asserting affirmative defenses such as lack of standing/ownership, failure of proof of assignment, no account stated, and improper interest/fees). Filing an Answer preserves every defense and costs you nothing in terms of rights; it does not admit the debt. After you answer you can serve a Demand for Bill of Particulars (Code Civ. Proc. § 454) if a book account is pleaded, and use discovery to make the debt buyer produce the cardholder agreement, the charge-off statement, and the complete chain of assignment from the original creditor to it — this is where debt-buyer cases most often fail. Most of these cases are 'collections cases' under Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.740, which has its own case-management timeline. Also check whether you qualify for a court fee waiver (form FW-001).

5) Whether the debt buyer can actually prove ownership and the amount is a merits question a judge decides case by case; I can't predict that outcome, and you should have a licensed California consumer attorney (or your county's self-help center / a legal aid office) review the complaint well before October 9, 2026. If the collector has made false statements in connection with collection, you may also have claims under the federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. § 1692e, 1692f) and California's Rosenthal Act (Civ. Code § 1788 et seq.) and the Fair Debt Buying Practices Act (Civ. Code §§ 1788.50–1788.64), which requires debt buyers to plead and possess specific documentation — worth having counsel check.

Bottom line: the 2-year oral-contract limit does not apply to an online credit card agreement; the applicable period is 4 years and it has not run; and you must file a written response by the October 9–12, 2026 window or risk a default judgment.

Based on the facts you've given, the suit appears to have been filed inside the four-year window, so it is most likely NOT time-barred.

The law: A suit on a written contract in California must be brought within four years. Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a). For an installment loan, the clock does not start on the date of your last payment — it starts when you actually breach, i.e., when a required payment comes due and is not made (and each later missed installment has its own four-year clock; if the lender accelerates, the clock on the accelerated balance runs from the acceleration).

The date math:
- Payments were due on the 15th of each month. Your last payment was made August 15, 2022 — so that installment was paid, and no breach occurred on that date.
- The first installment you did not pay was the one due September 15, 2022. That is the earliest date a cause of action could have accrued.
- September 15, 2022 + 4 years = September 15, 2026.
- The complaint is file-stamped September 2, 2026, which is 13 days BEFORE September 15, 2026. An action is commenced when the complaint is filed (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 312, 350).

So the claim on the first missed installment (and on every installment after it, and on any accelerated balance) was filed within four years. Note how close this is: if the accrual date were treated as August 15, 2022 (the last-payment date, which is the date collectors often use but which is not the legal accrual date here because that payment was made), the four years would have run on August 15, 2026 and the suit would be late. The distinction matters, so keep proof of the August 15, 2022 payment and of the September 15, 2022 due date.

Two things that could change this analysis, which you should check:
1. Whether you were already in default BEFORE August 15, 2022 — e.g., if you had missed an earlier installment that was never cured, or if the credit union accelerated the whole balance before September 2, 2022, the accrual date could be earlier and part or all of the claim could be outside four years. "Last payment August 15, 2022" does not by itself establish that you were current through that date.
2. California Emergency Rule 9 tolled limitations periods over 180 days from April 6, 2020 to October 1, 2020, but that only helps claims that existed during that window. Your claim accrued in 2022, so it does not apply. Nothing in your facts (no death, no absence from California, no bankruptcy) creates tolling under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 351 or 11 U.S.C. § 362 either.

Important practical point: the statute of limitations is an affirmative defense that is waived if you don't raise it, and it does not excuse you from responding to the lawsuit. In California you generally have 30 days after you are served with the summons and complaint to file a response (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 412.20(a)(3)); missing that deadline can result in a default judgment even if you have good defenses. You should still respond on time and raise any other defenses (amount owed, standing/chain of assignment, proof the assignee owns the loan, etc.). Whether any particular defense succeeds is a merits question for a licensed California attorney or your local legal-aid office.

answer.answer:
No — 25% is too much for an ordinary credit-card judgment in California. California law is more protective than the federal 25% rule, and where state law is more protective it controls (15 U.S.C. § 1677).

The governing statute, Code of Civil Procedure § 706.050 (as amended effective September 1, 2023), caps what can be taken on a non-support earnings withholding order at the LESSER of:
  (a) 20% of disposable earnings for the pay period, or
  (b) 40% of the amount by which disposable earnings for the pay period exceed 48 × the applicable hourly minimum wage (state minimum wage, or the local minimum wage at her worksite if that is higher) per week.
Because the levy is the *lesser* of the two, 25% can never be correct on a credit-card judgment — the old 25%/30× federal-minimum-wage formula is what employers used before September 1, 2023, and it sounds like her employer (or an outdated calculation) is still using it.

Doing the math on her $4,000 monthly disposable earnings, using the California state minimum wage of $16.90/hour in effect since January 1, 2026 (verify the current figure and any city/county minimum wage):
  • Prong (a): 20% × $4,000 = $800.00 per month.
  • Prong (b): weekly exempt floor = 48 × $16.90 = $811.20. Monthly conversion = 52 weeks ÷ 12 months = 4.3333 weeks per month, so $811.20 × 4.3333 = $3,515.20. Excess = $4,000.00 − $3,515.20 = $484.80. 40% × $484.80 = $193.92 per month.
  • Lesser of $800.00 and $193.92 = **about $193.92 per month**, not $1,000.

If she works in a city with a higher local minimum wage (e.g., Los Angeles, San Francisco, West Hollywood, Emeryville, many others), the exempt floor is *higher* and the garnishable amount is *lower* still — for example, at an $18.00 local minimum wage: 48 × $18.00 = $864.00/week × 4.3333 = $3,744.00; excess $256.00; 40% = $102.40 per month. So the exact dollar cap depends on the minimum wage applicable at her place of employment, but under every version of the calculation the $1,000 (25%) being withheld exceeds the legal maximum.

Two caveats: these caps assume (1) this is an ordinary money judgment, not a support or tax withholding order — you state there is no child- or spousal-support order, and support arrears orders can go higher under CCP § 706.052; and (2) no court order has modified the amount.

What she can do:
  • Give the employer/payroll a copy of the current CCP § 706.050 formula and the Judicial Council instructions that come with the Earnings Withholding Order (WG-002) and Employer's Return (WG-005); employers are required to withhold only the statutory maximum, and over-withholding should be corrected going forward.
  • File a Claim of Exemption (form WG-006, with Financial Statement WG-007/EJ-165) with the levying officer named on the order. Under CCP §§ 706.105 and 706.051 the judgment debtor may claim an exemption at any time while the order is in effect, including on the ground that some or all of the earnings are necessary for the support of her or her family. If the creditor opposes, a hearing is set and the amount the judge allows above the necessities-of-life exemption is discretionary — that merits question should go to a licensed California attorney or your local legal aid/self-help center.
  • Amounts already over-withheld: ask the levying officer and creditor to credit or refund the excess; a motion to the issuing court can be brought if they refuse.

Nothing here is a deadline that has passed — the claim of exemption route remains open while the withholding order is in effect.

answer.answer:
No — that's a misreading of California law, and the timing matters a lot, so act now.

1) The vehicle exemption is NOT automatic. Under Code of Civil Procedure § 703.510 and § 703.520, property levied on is protected only if the debtor files a written **claim of exemption** with the **levying officer (the sheriff who levied)**, using Judicial Council form EJ-160 (plus EJ-165 financial statement if required). If you do nothing, the exemption is treated as waived for this levy and the sheriff can proceed to sell the car.

2) Your deadline (personal service on 9/10/2026): § 703.520(a) gives you 10 days after service of the notice of levy. Counting under CCP § 12 (exclude the day of service, include the last day): Sept 11 = day 1 ... Sept 20 = day 10. September 20, 2026 falls on a Sunday, so under CCP §§ 12 and 12a the deadline rolls to **Monday, September 21, 2026**. Today is Sept 17, so you have about 4 days. Do not rely on the weekend roll-over — file by Friday, September 18, 2026 if you can, and get a file-stamped copy from the sheriff. (Note: had the notice been served by mail rather than personally, § 684.120 would have added 5 days; your facts say personal service, so the 10-day clock applies as computed.)

3) The exemption is a dollar cap on your equity, not blanket protection of 'one car.' CCP § 704.010 exempts only a specified dollar amount of equity in a motor vehicle (or in the aggregate for more than one). That figure is adjusted for inflation every three years under CCP § 703.150, most recently effective April 1, 2025 — confirm the exact current amount on Judicial Council form EJ-156 ('Current Dollar Amounts of Exemptions from Enforcement of Judgments') or from the sheriff/court clerk. It is in the low-thousands-of-dollars range, well under $15,000. Because your car is worth about $15,000 free and clear, your equity exceeds the cap, so a properly conducted execution sale can go forward even if you file the claim; § 704.010 then entitles you to be paid the exempt dollar amount out of the sale proceeds, and those proceeds are themselves exempt for 90 days after receipt. The phrase you read about 'one motor vehicle' refers to how the dollar cap is applied across vehicles, not to an automatic, unlimited exemption.

4) What happens after you file: the levying officer serves your claim on the judgment creditor; under § 703.550 the creditor has 10 days to file a notice of opposition and a motion for an order determining the claim, and the court then decides. Whether the court sustains or denies a claim, and any request to set aside or restrain the sale, is a discretionary judicial determination — I can't predict it, and you should take the merits to a licensed California attorney or your local self-help center. The hard deadline that you cannot miss is the claim-of-exemption filing described above.

5) Practical points to discuss with counsel quickly: whether the car is exempt on some other basis (e.g., a tool-of-the-trade theory under § 704.060 does not apply here since you don't use it in a trade or business), whether you can pay the creditor the non-exempt equity or negotiate to release the levy, and whether bankruptcy (where the alternative § 703.140(b) exemptions, including a 'wildcard,' become available) makes sense — you said you are not in bankruptcy, and those alternative exemptions are not available outside bankruptcy.

answer.answer:
No — the bank representative is wrong. California's automatic bank-account exemption is not a one-time-per-case or once-a-lifetime allowance; it applies to EVERY levy on your deposit account.

Why:

1. Code of Civil Procedure § 704.220 says that money in a judgment debtor's deposit account, in an amount equal to or less than the minimum basic standard of adequate care for a family of four for Region 1 (an amount set each year by the California Department of Social Services under Welf. & Inst. Code § 11452), 'is exempt without making a claim.' It is self-executing: the bank is required to leave that amount alone and turn over only the excess (see also CCP § 700.140 on levies against deposit accounts). Nothing in § 704.220 or in the levy statutes says the protection is used up once, or limits it to one levy per judgment, per creditor, or per year. Each new levy is a new levy on money that is in the account on that date, and the statutory floor has to be left in the account again. So when the creditor levied in September 2026, the bank should again have left the current (2026) Region 1 MBSAC-for-a-family-of-four amount and turned over only what was above it. (Confirm the current figure on the CDSS MBSAC schedule or the Judicial Council levy/exemption forms — it is indexed annually, so the 2026 number is higher than the February 2026... i.e., the same 2026 figure applies to both levies, and it is larger than earlier years' amounts.)

2. You may be entitled to MORE than the automatic minimum, because you say the balance was rebuilt from wages. Under CCP § 704.070, earnings that were paid to you and can be traced into your deposit account remain exempt to the same extent they would have been protected from wage garnishment (generally the large majority of them; 100% if they had been subject to a support withholding order). Under CCP § 704.225, money in a deposit account that is not otherwise exempt is exempt to the extent it is necessary for the support of you and your dependents. Unlike § 704.220, these two exemptions are NOT automatic — you must file a claim of exemption to get them.

3. What to do now, and the deadline that matters. To claim the wage-tracing and necessary-support exemptions, you must file a claim of exemption (Judicial Council form EJ-160, with a financial statement EJ-165 for § 704.225) with the levying officer (the sheriff/marshal named on the papers), not with the bank, within the short period set by CCP § 703.510–703.520. That period runs from the date the Notice of Levy was served on you — generally 10 days after service, and CCP § 684.120 adds 5 days if it was served by mail in California (10 days if mailed out of state); recent legislation has lengthened some of these enforcement-of-judgment notice periods, so use the deadline printed on the Notice of Levy you received. Example of the arithmetic: if the Notice of Levy was mailed to you in California on September 10, 2026, the count is 10 days to September 20, 2026, plus 5 days for mail service = September 25, 2026. Short answer: No. On the facts you describe, a credit-card judgment cannot be used to force the sale of your Fort Worth home, and the abstract of judgment does not attach as a valid lien against it.

Why:

1. Your property is an urban homestead. Under Tex. Prop. Code § 41.002(c), a homestead is 'urban' if it is within a municipality (or its extraterritorial jurisdiction) and is served by police protection, paid or volunteer fire protection, and at least three of the following municipal utilities: electric, natural gas, sewer, storm sewer, and water. Your lot is inside the Fort Worth city limits with city water, sewer, electricity, and police and fire service — that satisfies the test. An urban family homestead may be up to 10 acres of contiguous lots with improvements (§ 41.002(a)). Your 0.3 acre is far under that limit, and the entire value is protected — Texas places no dollar cap on homestead value for a judgment creditor like this one. Homestead status is automatic in Texas from occupancy and use as a home; no filing is required (a voluntary designation is optional under § 41.005).

2. A credit-card judgment is not one of the debts that can reach a homestead. Tex. Const. art. XVI, § 50(a) and Tex. Prop. Code § 41.001(b) allow forced sale of a homestead only for: purchase money, ad valorem taxes on the property, an owelty of partition (including a divorce-related lien), refinance of a federal tax lien, a written home-improvement contract signed by both spouses, a home-equity loan meeting the constitutional requirements, a reverse mortgage, a manufactured-home conversion/refinance, and a few other narrow categories. You say there is no mortgage, no tax lien, no home-improvement contract, no home-equity loan and no bankruptcy. An unsecured credit-card judgment is not on that list.

3. The abstract of judgment does not create an enforceable lien on the homestead. Under Tex. Prop. Code § 52.0012, a recorded abstract of judgment does not attach to homestead property. It can still show up as a cloud on title when you sell or refinance. Texas gives you a self-help fix: you (or your title company/attorney) send the judgment creditor and its attorney of record a notice letter with the proposed homestead affidavit by certified mail, and then, no earlier than the 31st day after the letter is mailed, record the homestead affidavit as a release of the judgment lien. The release becomes effective unless the creditor timely records a contradicting affidavit. Many people do this at closing; a real-estate or consumer attorney or title company can handle it.

4. What the creditor CAN still do: collect from non-exempt property — bank accounts (by writ of garnishment), non-exempt vehicles beyond the exemption, and similar assets. Texas wages, however, are generally not subject to garnishment for an ordinary consumer debt (Tex. Const. art. XVI, § 28; Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 63.004), though funds can be seized once deposited. Also, if you ever sell the homestead, the sale proceeds are exempt for six months after the sale (Tex. Prop. Code § 41.001(c)). Separately, a Texas judgment goes dormant if no writ of execution issues within 10 years, and can be revived within 2 years of dormancy (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §§ 34.001, 31.006).

5. The collector's threat may itself be unlawful. Threatening to take an action that cannot legally be taken — such as forcing the sale of a protected Texas homestead — can violate the federal FDCPA, 15 U.S.C. § 1692e(5) and § 1692e(10), and the Texas Debt Collection Act, Tex. Fin. Code § 392.301(a)(8) (threatening to take an action prohibited by law), enforceable under § 392.403 (actual damages, injunctive relief, attorney's fees). Deadline math: an FDCPA claim must be filed within one year of the violation (15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d)). You did not give me the date the collector made the statement, so I cannot compute the exact cutoff — count one year forward from the date of that call or letter (for example, a statement made on 2026-09-17 would have to be sued on by 2027-09-17; one made on 2026-01-10 by 2027-01-10). TDCA claims generally carry a longer limitations period, but do not rely on that without counsel. Whether a court would find a violation and what damages would follow is a discretionary merits call — have a Texas consumer attorney review the actual recording, letter, or call notes. Save all voicemails, letters, and call logs now.

Bottom line: they cannot force the sale of your homestead on this credit-card judgment, and you can clear the abstract from your title using the § 52.0012 homestead-affidavit procedure. Verify with the Tarrant County real property records whether an abstract of judgment has in fact been filed.

answer.answer:
Short answer: No — the $50,000 figure does not work the way you are hoping, and a taxable brokerage account of publicly traded stock is generally NOT exempt in Texas.

Why:

1. The $50,000 is a value CEILING, not a wildcard. Tex. Prop. Code § 42.001(a) says personal property described in § 42.002 is exempt up to an aggregate fair market value of $50,000 for a single adult with no dependents ($100,000 for a family). The property must first fall into one of the categories listed in § 42.002 before the dollar cap even matters. Texas does not have a general 'any property you choose' wildcard exemption outside of bankruptcy.

2. Stocks, brokerage accounts and cash are not on the § 42.002 list. The listed categories are things like home furnishings (including heirlooms), food/provisions, farming and ranching vehicles and implements, tools, equipment, books and apparatus of a trade or profession, wearing apparel, jewelry (capped at 25% of the total exemption), two firearms, athletic and sporting equipment, one two-, three- or four-wheeled motor vehicle for each licensed driver in the household, certain livestock and pets, and unpaid commissions for personal services (capped at 25%). A general taxable investment account is not in any of those categories, so the $50,000 cap never comes into play for it.

3. Separate statutes protect some financial assets — but you have already ruled them out. Tex. Prop. Code § 42.0021 exempts qualified retirement accounts (IRA, 401(k), 403(b), certain HSAs), § 42.0022 exempts qualified 529/college savings plans, and Tex. Ins. Code § 1108.051 exempts life insurance and annuity cash values. You say this is an ordinary taxable brokerage account, not a retirement account, so none of these apply.

4. Your furniture, clothes and one car ARE in exempt categories (home furnishings under § 42.002(a)(1), wearing apparel under § 42.002(a)(5), one motor vehicle under § 42.002(a)(9)), subject to the $50,000 aggregate cap. Ironically, having only $30,000 of exempt-category property does not let you 'use up' the remaining $20,000 on stock.

What this means practically: the creditor's writ of garnishment on the brokerage firm can reach the stock account, and a judgment creditor can also use the turnover statute, Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 31.002, to compel you to turn over non-exempt assets like securities.

Deadlines you must not miss (I do not have the service dates, so check the papers you received):
- Under Tex. R. Civ. P. 663a, you must be served with a copy of the writ, the application, the accompanying affidavits and the court's order.
- Under Tex. R. Civ. P. 664a, you may file a sworn motion to dissolve or modify the writ at ANY time before judgment in the garnishment suit, and the court must set a hearing within 10 days of filing and rule within 10 days after the hearing. Because that clock is tied to the garnishment judgment, waiting is dangerous.
- The garnishee (your brokerage) must file an answer by the appearance day stated in the writ, which under Tex. R. Civ. P. 659 and the general citation rule is the Monday next after 20 days from service. Example of the arithmetic only (I do not know your actual service date): if the writ were served on the brokerage on Sept. 17, 2026, then 17 Sept + 20 days = Oct. 7, 2026, and the Monday next following is Oct. 12, 2026 — that would be the answer date, and a default judgment against the garnishee could follow soon after. Substitute your real service date to get your real dates.

Things still worth checking with a Texas attorney right away (today is Sept. 17, 2026):
- Whether any money in the account is traceable to a protected source (e.g., a rollover from an IRA/401(k) that keeps its § 42.0021 character, life insurance or annuity proceeds under Ins. Code § 1108.051, current wages under § 42.001(b)(1), Social Security or other federal benefits, or personal-injury/workers' comp proceeds), which can change the analysis for that portion.
- Whether the judgment itself is valid as to you (proper service, correct defendant, dormancy, satisfaction, or an active appeal/supersedeas).
- Whether Chapter 7 or 13 bankruptcy helps. In bankruptcy a Texas filer may elect the federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(2)/(d) instead of Texas exemptions; the federal scheme has a wildcard (§ 522(d)(5)) that could shelter part — but nowhere near all — of $30,000 in stock. That is a fact-specific decision with its own risks.

Bottom line: do not rely on the $50,000 number to protect the brokerage account. Treat the account as at risk and get a Texas consumer/debtor's-rights attorney involved before the answer date on the writ.

No — that 14-day rule is the justice court rule, and you were not sued in a justice court. Nothing has been lost.

1) Which rule applies. In Texas, the 14-day answer deadline comes from the Rules for Justice Court Cases (Tex. R. Civ. P. 500.3, 502.5), which apply to suits filed in a justice of the peace court (small-claims track, jurisdictional limit $20,000 exclusive of interest and costs, Tex. Gov't Code § 27.031). Your citation is captioned 'County Court at Law No. 2, Tarrant County' — a statutory county court, not a justice court. County and district courts follow Tex. R. Civ. P. 99(b): the answer is due 'by 10:00 a.m. on the Monday next after the expiration of twenty days after' the date of service. The dollar amount of the suit ($6,000) does not change which rule applies; the court in which it was filed does.

2) Your actual deadline, computed. Service date: Tuesday, September 1, 2026. Under Rule 4 you do not count the day of service, so the 20-day period runs September 2 through September 21, 2026. September 1, 2026 is a Tuesday, so September 21, 2026 is a Monday. The 20 days therefore expire on Monday, September 21, and the 'Monday next after the expiration of twenty days' is Monday, September 28, 2026. Your written answer is due by 10:00 a.m. on Monday, September 28, 2026. As of today, Thursday, September 17, 2026, you have 11 days left. (Before relying on my math, read the deadline language printed on the face of your citation and confirm it with the Tarrant County clerk — the citation itself states the deadline, and clerks' offices will confirm it.)

3) Even a missed deadline is not the end. Under Tex. R. Civ. P. 239, a default judgment can only be taken if no answer is on file. Texas courts have long held that a late answer filed before the court signs a default judgment defeats the default. You say no default judgment has been signed, so filing an answer now — today, if you can — protects you. And if a default were ever entered, you would still have 30 days from the date the judgment is signed to file a motion for new trial (Tex. R. Civ. P. 320, 329b).

4) Practical next steps. File a short written answer with the county clerk that (a) denies the plaintiff's allegations (a general denial is allowed by Tex. R. Civ. P. 92), and (b) pleads any affirmative defenses you may have — for example, limitations (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Short answer: No — please don't ignore it. The belief that "Texas never allows wage garnishment" is only half right, and acting on it could cost you money you can't get back.

What Texas law actually says: Texas does protect current wages for personal services from garnishment by ordinary private creditors (Tex. Const. art. XVI, § 28; Tex. Prop. Code § 42.001(b)(1); Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 63.004). So a collector or debt buyer holding a judgment on your old credit-card account generally cannot reach your paycheck in Texas. But that protection has express exceptions: court-ordered child support, court-ordered spousal maintenance, federal tax levies, and — critically for you — garnishments authorized by federal law, which override the Texas exemption under the Supremacy Clause. Federal administrative wage garnishment does not require a lawsuit, a judgment, or a Texas court order, and it does not care that Texas has a wage exemption.

Why the "15%" number matters: 15% of disposable pay is the exact statutory cap for (a) defaulted federal student loans under 20 U.S.C. § 1095a(a)(1) and 34 C.F.R. § 34.19, and (b) other nontax federal debts under the Debt Collection Improvement Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3720D and 31 C.F.R. § 285.11. That is a strong hint that this is a federal student-loan garnishment (ED, a guaranty agency, or Treasury cross-servicing) — which would be lawful in Texas. An IRS levy usually is not a flat 15% (it uses exemption tables, 26 U.S.C. §§ 6331, 6334), and a state-court writ for a credit card would normally not be 15% of a Texas employee's wages at all.

I can't tell you whether this particular order is lawful until you know who issued it, so here is what each answer would mean:
• If it is a federal administrative wage garnishment on your defaulted federal student loan (or another federal debt): it is legal in Texas, your employer must comply, and ignoring it accomplishes nothing. Your remedies are administrative — request a hearing to object to the existence/amount of the debt or to claim financial hardship (34 C.F.R. §§ 34.6–34.8; 31 C.F.R. § 285.11(f)). Timing is critical: if you request the hearing in writing within 30 days of the date on the garnishment notice the agency sent you, the garnishment is generally stayed until the hearing officer rules; a later request still gets you a hearing, but the withholding usually continues in the meantime. Date arithmetic: today is 2026-09-17, and 2026-09-17 minus 30 days = 2026-08-18. So if the notice is dated on or after 2026-08-18, a written hearing request sent immediately is still timely; if it is dated before 2026-08-18, request the hearing anyway (it is not barred, it just may not stop the withholding). You may also be able to stop the garnishment entirely by getting out of default through consolidation or an income-driven rehabilitation/repayment arrangement — ask the holder. Note that federal student loans have no statute of limitations (20 U.S.C. § 1091a), so "it's old" is not a defense.
• If it is a state-court writ of garnishment obtained by the credit-card creditor or a debt buyer: then your current wages are almost certainly exempt, and the proper move is not to ignore it but to file a motion to dissolve or modify the writ and assert the wage exemption (Tex. R. Civ. P. 664a; Tex. Const. art. XVI, § 28). You would also want to know whether a default judgment was entered against you and whether you were ever properly served. (Do not assume the credit-card debt is time-barred; Texas's four-year limitations period, Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 16.004, is measured from default, and I have no dates for it.)

Do these things now, before the next payroll run:
1. Ask payroll in writing, today, for a copy of every page they received, including the issuing agency/court name, case or account number, the date on the order, and the contact address. Your employer has it; you are entitled to see what is being applied to your pay.
2. Check your own mail and your federal student aid records — federal law requires the agency to send you written notice at least 30 days before garnishment begins, and that notice contains the hearing-request deadline and form.
3. Preserve the notice date. Deadlines here run from the date of that notice, not from the date payroll told you.
4. One more caution: even where wages are exempt, Texas courts have held that the current-wages exemption is generally lost once the wages are deposited into a bank account, so a judgment creditor may still try to garnish the account. That is a separate issue from your paycheck.

Because whether this specific garnishment is enforceable turns entirely on who issued it, get the paperwork and then have a Texas consumer attorney or a legal aid office review it — many will review a garnishment packet quickly, and the federal hearing request is something you can file yourself in the meantime to protect the 30-day window.

Short answer: probably not on those facts — and not because you waited too long, but because of *how* the FCRA is structured. Here is why, and what to do about it.

1) The FCRA's investigation duty that consumers can enforce in court is triggered by the credit bureaus, not by you. Under 15 U.S.C. § 1681s-2(b), a furnisher (here, the collection agency) must conduct a reasonable investigation, review the information you supplied, and correct or delete inaccurate information — but that duty only kicks in after the furnisher receives notice of the dispute *from a consumer reporting agency* (Equifax, Experian or TransUnion). You told us you have never disputed this item with any of the three bureaus, so no § 1681s-2(b) duty has ever been triggered, and there is nothing yet for the agency to have breached.

2) A dispute sent directly to the collector falls under § 1681s-2(a) and its 'direct dispute' regulation (12 C.F.R. § 1022.43), which does require furnishers to investigate certain direct disputes. But 15 U.S.C. § 1681s-2(c) and (d) expressly strip consumers of a private right of action for § 1681s-2(a) violations — only the CFPB, FTC, and state officials can enforce that subsection. So the 60 days of silence, standing alone, is not something you can sue over under the FCRA.

Date math: 60 days before today (2026-09-17) is 2026-07-19 (Sept 17 minus 17 days = Aug 31; minus 31 more = Jul 31; minus 12 more = Jul 19, 2026). That is the approximate mailing date of your direct dispute. Nothing about that date bars you from anything — no FCRA deadline has run. The FCRA statute of limitations is the earlier of 2 years from when you discover the violation or 5 years from the violation (15 U.S.C. § 1681p), and the violation you would want to sue on has not even been triggered yet.

3) What to do to create an enforceable FCRA claim: dispute the account in writing with each of Equifax, Experian and TransUnion (online or by certified mail), attaching your proof of payment. Keep copies and proof of delivery. The bureau then has 30 days to investigate (45 days if you supply additional information during the initial 30-day window) under 15 U.S.C. § 1681i(a)(1), and it must forward your dispute and all relevant information to the collection agency (§ 1681i(a)(2)). At that point § 1681s-2(b) applies to the agency. If the agency then 'verifies' the debt as unpaid without a reasonable investigation, or fails to correct the reporting, you have a private claim against the furnisher under §§ 1681n (willful) and 1681o (negligent), and potentially against the bureau under § 1681i. Your existing 60-day-old direct dispute and its proof of payment are still valuable evidence that the agency's later investigation was unreasonable or willful.

4) Separate from the FCRA, look at the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act. If this agency qualifies as a 'debt collector' under 15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6), reporting a paid debt as unpaid can violate § 1692e(8) (communicating credit information known or that should be known to be false) and § 1692e(2)(A) (false representation of the character or amount of the debt). The FDCPA's deadline is one year from the violation (15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d)); many courts treat each false monthly report to the bureaus as its own violation, so if false reporting has occurred within the past year that claim may be live. Whether this particular company is a covered 'debt collector' and exactly when it last transmitted the false status are facts a lawyer would need to confirm.

Bottom line: don't sue yet on the ignored direct dispute. File bureau disputes now — that is the step that converts your evidence into an enforceable FCRA claim — and have a consumer-law attorney evaluate a parallel FDCPA claim for the false 'unpaid' reporting.
